newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr squeezed by shrinking yield spreads.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr squeezed by shrinking yield spreads.

text.p: The Australian dollar suffered its fourth straight lower close Thursday as a shrinking interest rate advantage sent investors looking elsewhere for a home.

Traders said bears did not have everything their own way and bidding had been strong, mainly from Asia, under US$0.7720. However, strong industrial production data from the U.S. had made it more likely than ever that rates there would rise, in contrast to Australia where all the talk was of another easing.
Whether a cut was a real possibility may become clearer next week after the government announced the ruling on a crucial national minimum wage claim would be delivered on Tuesday.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar was fealing the heat at US$0.7720/25 after melting from an early US$0.7740/45 and US$0.7745/50 late here Wednesday.

Analysts noted the currency was oversold on daily charts after sliding all the way from a US$0.7895 peak on Friday and felt this was probably not a favourable time to actively short it. They did, however, recommend selling into any rally around US$0.7785, with a stop at US$0.7820 resistance.
On the downside, a break of US$0.7680 would confirm a more meaningful downtrend was underway which could see the dollar revisit the February 12 low at US$0.7550.
On the crosses it fled to 96.62/72 yen from 97.55/65 late Wednesday, with a retreat in the U.S. dollar encouraging a Japanese impulse to take profits.

The U.S. dollar slid to 124.20/25 yen from an early 125.90/95 after Japan reported its trade surplus with the U.S. jumped 11.2 percent in March, stirring concerns it may ignite long-dormant trade frictions between the two countries.
The softness was reflected in the local dollar's trade weighted index which dipped to 60.0 from 60.2 late Wednesday.
The currency did find some support from confirmation a large Victorian power station was about to be sold to offshore bids.

One source told Reuters the sale of the 2,000 megawatt station and associated coal mine was likely to fetch around A$4.5 billion for the state government, implying some requirement by the bidders to buy Australian dollar.
There was also much talk the sale of three Federal airports was near completion and that could invole up to A$3.0 billion.

However, the local currency had a major handicap in that its interest advantage over the U.S. dollar been steadily disappearing for the last few weeks and had actually turned negative for one and two year bonds. Shorter dates could go the same way if U.S. rates were hiked again in May as many expected.

The chance of a tightening by the Federal Reserve had been boosted by Wednesday's strong 0.9 percent rise in U.S. industrial production. In contrast, recent Australian data had made many here think another easing might be possible.

Domestic money market rates and bond yields had eased as a result and further narrowed the A$'s premium over the U.S. currency. Whether a cut was a real prospect may be clearer next Tuesday after the long-awaited verdict on a Living Wage claim by Australia's unions is delivered.
The RBA has warned that if the full claim was granted it would be inconsistent with the maintenance of low inflation.
The unions have asked for an immediate 8.75 percent increase in award wages and three A$20 per week pay rises over three years.
The government, however, has proposed the tribunal raise low-pay awards by A$8 a week each year for the next three years, a proposition backed by the RBA.
Analysts reckoned the central bank could swallow an award of A$11 to A$15 a week but anything more would alarm and probably end any chance of another policy easing this year.
The lower the actual result, therefore, the more bearish it would be for the dollar. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 3673 1800
